conceptTag: Sell software to a small firm
readerTitle: Fifteen minutes between lunch and dinner
caseNote: 가상 사례 (식당에 근무표 소프트웨어 판매, 소프트웨어 스튜디오에 케이터링 판매) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 작은 회사에 팔 때는 기능을 다 보여주는 것보다, 지난주에 실제로 무슨 일이 있었는지 묻고 그 문제 하나를 함께 풀어보는 다음 단계를 잡는 것이 판매를 만든다.
misconception: 작은 회사 사장은 바쁘니까 짧고 화려한 데모와 할인으로 그 자리에서 결정하게 만들어야 한다.

sources.text: SAL-01 유닛의 개념 레슨(Discovery, Closing) 적용
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 식당 사례의 수치(직원 12명, 일요일 저녁 2시간, 하루 약 3건의 근무 교대 메시지, 지난달 금요일 결근 1건)는 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 실제 통계처럼 읽히지 않는지 확인하세요.
케이터링 사례(직원 15명 소프트웨어 스튜디오, 주간 점심)는 가상 사례입니다. 카드에 illustrative 표시를 확인하세요.

cards.title: Fifteen minutes between lunch and dinner
body: Maria runs a busy family restaurant with 12 staff. The schedule lives on a whiteboard by the kitchen door and in a noisy group chat.
You sell staff scheduling software. She has agreed to meet you at 3:30, after the lunch rush and before dinner prep. You have about fifteen minutes, and she is still wiping down the counter.

image.label: Restaurant owner at a quiet counter, a whiteboard schedule behind her
image.brief: 점심과 저녁 사이 한산한 식당. 카운터를 닦는 사장님 뒤로 지우고 다시 쓴 흔적이 많은 화이트보드 근무표. 테이블 위에 노트북을 든 영업 담당자가 앉아 있음. 따뜻한 오후 햇빛. 실제 브랜드 로고 없음.

cards.title: How do you use the first five minutes?
body: Your software has shift planning, time clocks, payroll export, swap requests and a mobile app. Maria looks tired and a little skeptical.

options.text: Open the laptop and walk her through the main features quickly
options.feedback: You cover a lot, but you're guessing which features matter. Most of the time goes to things she doesn't need.

options.text: Ask her to tell you how last week's schedule went, and what went wrong
options.feedback: This is **discovery**: learning her real problem before offering anything. You give up demo time and gain the one thing the demo should be about.

options.text: Hand over the price sheet so she knows it's affordable
options.feedback: Busy owners do care about price. But a price means little before she sees what problem it solves for her.

cards.title: The schedule wasn't the real problem.
body: Making the schedule is fine. The pain is everything that happens *after* it's posted. And her head chef handles most swaps, so he will use the tool more than she will.

breakdown.label: Missed Friday shift
breakdown.detail: Last month, nobody saw the swap

cards.title: One person decides, and she has no spare time.
body: In a small firm, the owner is often the buyer, the payer and part of the support team. There is no IT department to set things up and no committee to persuade.
That cuts both ways. A decision can happen fast. But if the next step feels like extra work, it simply never happens. Your job is to make the next step small and clearly useful.

image.label: One person holding several hats: buyer, payer, user
image.brief: 한 사람이 모자 세 개를 겹쳐 쓴 일러스트. 각 모자에 "Buyer", "Payer", "Setup" 라벨. 옆에 시계가 거의 비어 있는 모습으로 시간 부족을 표현. 로고 없음.

cards.title: "Sounds useful. Send me something and I'll think about it."
body: The fifteen minutes are almost up. Maria is friendly but already looking toward the kitchen. What do you say?

options.text: "Of course. I'll email a brochure and check in in two weeks."
options.feedback: It's polite and low-pressure, but nothing is agreed. A brochure lands in a busy inbox and the deal quietly fades.

options.text: "Can we set up next week's schedule together on Tuesday at 3:30, with your head chef? Then you decide."
options.feedback: This is **closing**: asking for a clear next step that fits where she is. It costs her one quiet hour and shows the tool on her own swap problem.

options.text: "If you sign today, I can take 30% off the first year."
options.feedback: It might win a fast yes. But it pushes a decision before she's seen the value, and it teaches her your price is soft.

cards.title: Close on the next step, not the whole deal.
body: Maria wasn't ready to buy. She was ready to try one thing that would save her a Sunday evening.

Discovery told you what that thing was: swaps the head chef can approve from his phone. Closing turned it into a date, a time and the right two people in the room. On Tuesday, the tool either fixes her real problem or it doesn't. Either way, you both learn fast.

cards.title: Sometimes the helpful answer is no.
body: If Maria had five staff and no swap problems, the whiteboard might be the better tool. Selling it anyway wins a customer who cancels in three months and tells other owners.
Small firms also feel setup pain sharply. Promise only what you can deliver in that first hour. A small promise kept beats a big one that slips.

cards.title: Now you're the one selling food.
body: You run a catering business. The office manager at a 15-person software studio emails: "What would weekly team lunches cost?"

options.text: Reply with your full menu and price list right away
options.feedback: Fast and clear, but it turns you into one quote among many. You don't yet know what these lunches are for.

options.text: Ask what the lunches are for, who decides and any diet needs, then offer one trial Friday with a date
options.feedback: **Discovery** finds the real job, maybe getting a remote team in on the same day. **Closing** turns interest into a booked Friday.

options.text: Offer a free lunch for the whole team this week
options.feedback: Generous, but you're spending money before knowing what they need or who approves the budget.

cards.softwareNote: Studios like this often decide in a team chat. Asking who signs off on spending can matter as much as asking what they like to eat.

cards.title: Ask about last week, then agree on next week.
body: **Concepts used:** *Discovery* found the real pain behind the request. *Closing* turned a vague "send me something" into one small, dated step with the right people.
**Try it today:** think of a prospect who said "let me think about it." Write one question about what went wrong for them last week, and one specific next step you could ask for.
